reading.title: Separating categories from brands
reading.text: A product-literacy worksheet distinguishes categories and branded names. Vodka is a distilled spirit; gin emphasizes juniper flavor, rum derives from sugarcane products, and tequila is an agave spirit under relevant rules. Whiskey concerns distilled grain products. Bourbon and Scotch have distinct product requirements; Scotch is produced in Scotland. Brandy comes from wine or fermented fruit products, while Cognac is a protected geographical designation. Mezcal is an agave spirit, not a cactus. Triple sec and amaretto describe liqueur types. Kahlúa, Baileys and Grand Marnier are branded names. The trainee checks the producer's information rather than infers identity from color or bottle shape. The lesson reads labels and categories without offering a purchase recommendation, serving instruction or claim that all products within a category taste alike.

reading.title: Reading a mixer list
reading.text: The next list contains both branded products and other beverage terms. Chartreuse, Campari, Aperol, Drambuie and Cointreau are branded liqueur or aperitif names with different product descriptions. Tonic water contains quinine flavoring, while soda water is carbonated water. Ginger beer has ginger character, but its alcohol content varies by product. Cola is a soft drink, and cranberry juice is a fruit drink. Orange juice and lime juice come from different citrus fruits. Simple syrup names dissolved sugar in water; grenadine is a sweet red syrup traditionally associated with pomegranate. Bitters is a flavoring category that may contain alcohol. The trainee checks composition and alcohol information on the actual product. A familiar name, color or garnish is insufficient to establish alcohol-free status, ingredients or suitability.

reading.title: Naming garnish shapes
reading.text: The trainee examines a food-decoration display. A lemon twist is a strip of lemon peel; a lime wedge is a wedge-shaped piece of lime. Orange peel names the fruit's outer covering, and cherry names the fruit rather than wood. An olive is another small fruit. A mint sprig is a stem with mint leaves; cinnamon stick is rolled dried bark. Salt rim and sugar rim name different coatings around a glass edge. A cocktail umbrella is a tiny paper decoration. The trainee compares shapes before reading the composition record. White crystals are not reliably identified as salt or sugar by a photograph, and a colored fruit piece does not establish allergens or product treatment. The display teaches terms without mixing, tasting or requiring an alcoholic beverage.
